VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Mulla Sadra is preparing to take a decisive step: “Now, to show that the persons of the Imams are the Treasures of God's knowledge—that is, that by being what God knows, in and through their act of knowing Him, they are both the Treasures and their Keepers—requires two higher sources, or rather, two sublime oceans from the ocean of knowledge disclosed in mystical divination ...” And here the flight is broken off. The sentence was never finished.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Yet we can glimpse the metaphysical summit toward which Mulla Sadra's understanding of the Imam was moving. Other Shiite philosophers of divine wisdom lived long enough to approach it and to say what can be said of it by following, step by step, the Imams' own allusions. Everything in the foregoing pages has sought to draw on their teaching.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
Indeed, the Imams' own words about the A'râf already help us understand how what is said of the “Perfect Words” applies to the Imams too.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Our sketch of some essential features of Shiism can thus end, for the time being, where it began. All that has been said in these pages, compared with the great works of Shiite spiritual philosophy, is no more than a drop in the ocean. I have referred several times to a small private study circle in Tehran.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

To bring this part of the book to a close, I want to recall one more evening there, a memorable evening in the autumn of 1964. Our discussion was devoted to the recurring theme of Shiite theology, the theme that has guided us throughout the preceding chapters: Tawhîd, the affirmation of God's oneness, and the Imam. How can Tawhîd be realized in its full truth—escaping the twin dangers of ta'tîl and tashbîh—except through the existence of the Imam?
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

At the end of the evening, we listened as the venerable Shaykh M. H. T., whose knowledge of Mulla Sadra's philosophy was exceptionally deep, brought his meditation aloud to something like a conclusion: “All the Names and Attributes we give to God—or rather, that God gives to Himself in revealing Himself to us—are made possible only by the figure of the eternal Imam, who gathers them all into himself.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
“At the height of our spiritual states, these Names and Attributes may be absorbed into the inner human being. That person is no longer himself: the Imam becomes that person.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

“But God in Himself remains unknowable and beyond our reach. The Imam is the living, eternal reality, a hidden immaterial splendor, our immaterial bond with the immaterial. He is that Face of God of which the Quranic verses (55:26–27) declare: Everything on earth is passing away, but the Face of your Lord endures, surrounded by splendor.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

To conclude, our shaykh recalled the famous final episode of the birds' pilgrimage in the great mystical epic by Farid al-Din Attar, Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds, twelfth century), one of the masterpieces of Persian mystical poetry. Thousands of birds set out as pilgrims. For years upon years they travel, crossing mountain heights and plunging into abysses.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Almost all are lost in the dramatic trials along the way. Only a few—thirty birds in all—reach the sublime goal and find themselves before the mysterious bird called Sîmorgh, symbol of the distant divinity. Its name goes back to the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrian Persia, and it reappears in the heroic and mystical epics of medieval Persia (below, Book II).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

In Persian, Attar's mystical genius brings a delicate play on words into its name: Sîmorgh can be read as sî morgh, “thirty birds.” And so, at the end of their long and painful quest, Sîmorgh becomes the mirror that reveals to the thirty survivors the mystery of their own being. When they look toward Sîmorgh, it is Sîmorgh they see.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

When they contemplate themselves, what they see is again sî morgh, thirty birds. And when they look both ways at once, Sîmorgh and sî morgh are one and the same reality. There are, in a sense, two Sîmorghs, and yet Sîmorgh is one. Identity within difference; difference within identity. Meister Eckhart, for his part, said: “The gaze by which I know Him is the very gaze by which He knows me.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

When we reached the end of Attar's famous verses, I asked the shaykh, “That is the Imam, is it not?” “Certainly, that is it. And if there were no Imam, if this were not the Imam, nothing would remain but to sink into mystical intoxication, expressed in the famous cry of the Sufi al-Hallaj: Anâ'l-Haqq! ‘I am God!’ ...”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

We have already seen how the experience of walâyat, the bond of spiritual love and guidance, makes Shiism, in its essence, a religion of love. Perhaps we can now sense again how the Imam keeps the mystic from losing his balance in an ecstasy whose paradoxical cry retains, despite every later recantation, a Luciferian echo.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

What the mystic can say is what the believer says in the Gnostic Acts of Peter: Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui—“I saw Him as I was able to grasp Him.” He showed Himself to me in the form my own being had the capacity to receive. Nothing more and nothing less.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
Yet this very correspondence, the immense grace of it, is precisely what the Shiite vision of the Imam means.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

We can now understand why Shiite spirituality does not experience the gulf that has troubled so many speculative Christian mystics: the gulf between the idea of the eternal Christ and the historical reality of Christ, with the divinity's “self-emptying” (exinanitio)—extending even to the cry that “God is dead.” That same evening our shaykh said: “Glory be to God!
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

“In our Shiite Islam, the Imams have reflected the eternal Imam. They are his mirrors, his mazâhir, the forms in which he is revealed. Their task is not to awaken us to consciousness of this world. Their walâyat is not an institution belonging to this world. They are our spiritual bond with the spiritual universes. They open the way for us to ascend, so that the veils may fall—the very veils they themselves have deliberately kept in place, lest the weak misunderstand what is meant by their divine qualification.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

We shall need to remember all these teachings in the final book of this work, devoted to the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Some of our Shiite authors have recognized in him the Saoshyant, the saving hero of Zoroastrian Iran; others have recognized the Paraclete foretold in the Gospel of John.

Within the Islamic community, the Iranian world has, from the beginning, formed a distinct whole. Its character and vocation can only be understood if we regard Iran's spiritual universe as a unity extending across the centuries before and after Islam. Islamic Iran has been, more than anywhere else, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears and its practical consequences—not primarily in the social world, but in the concrete whole that a human being nourishes with his own substance beyond the limits of this life: his spiritual world.

The great work Henry Corbin presents here, in four volumes comprising seven books, is the result of more than twenty years of research carried out in Iran itself. His method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school. He seeks to encounter religious experience by allowing its object to reveal itself as it reveals itself to those who experience it.

The phenomenologist must therefore become the spiritual guest of those to whom that reality appears, and share with them the responsibility of receiving it. Historical considerations will consequently remain within the world of the religious object itself, rather than imposing an alien category from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise.

The first volume (Book I) sets out several essential aspects of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which was firmly established in Iran from early times and became the official religion in the sixteenth century. The inquiry begins with what the author has proposed to call “the phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to those whom the Quran calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book,” embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
The second volume (Book II), published at the same time, examines Suhrawardi and the Platonists of Persia.

Mohammad ibn 'Alî ibn Abî Jomhûr Ahsâ'î was one of the great Imami thinkers of the ninth–tenth Islamic centuries (d. after 901/1496). For his statement about the essence of Shiism, see his major work Kitâb al-Mojlî, Tehran, 1324, p. 480. The same teaching can be found in Haydar Âmolî a century earlier, and our authors invariably appeal to statements by the Imams themselves in its support. We must stress from the outset that, in a Shiite context, we consistently use the term walâyat, not wilâyat, the word commonly used in Sufism. In Western writing these terms are often confused and inadequately translated as “sainthood.” Walâyat describes the Imams as God's Friends, Beloved Ones, or those brought close to God (walî Allâh; plural Awliyâ' Allâh). One can immediately see why the mystery of this divine election and sanctification lies at the very heart of the prophetic mission (nobowwat): every prophet (nabî) is a walî, but not every walî is entrusted with prophecy. The fundamental meaning of walâyat is “friendship” (Persian dûstî), and the word is frequently paired with mahabba (love, devoted affection). It also names the love and devotion Shiites bear toward their twelve Imams. For the believer, walâyat toward the Imam is a participation in the Imam's eternal walâyat. In the metaphysical framework of the teaching about the Imams, walâyat has a cosmic meaning and function, revealing itself on different levels of the universe. Wilâyat, in the usual Sufi sense, refers essentially to the mystic's subjective spiritual states. To trace the move from walâyat to wilâyat, and to ask whether one can speak of wilâyat while remaining silent about walâyat, is to raise the whole question of the relationship between Shiism and non-Shiite Sufism. That question would require a book of its own (see vol. III, Book IV below). In any event, the question of prophecy raised here and throughout this book must be understood in terms of nobowwat and walâyat: walâyat is “the esoteric (bâtin), inward reality of prophecy.” ↩
